paragraphs: This paper provides a mathematical foundation for the softassign quadratic assignment algorithm, an optimization method used in pattern recognition and combinatorial problems. Its central question concerns convergence: whether the algorithm's repeated updates approach a limiting result. That question is distinct from whether the method produces useful answers in individual applications.

The motivation is a gap between practical evidence and theoretical understanding. The algorithm had already appeared effective across thousands of simulations, but those observations did not constitute a convergence proof. Successful runs can establish that a method works in many tested situations; a proof establishes a property through mathematical reasoning about the algorithm.

The stated contribution is a convergence proof covering the algorithm's most general form. This gives its observed effectiveness a firmer theoretical basis without restricting the contribution to one application or simulation setting. The result should be read specifically as a convergence guarantee: the abstract does not identify convergence with finding the globally best assignment. Its significance is establishing a previously unproved property of an already useful optimization procedure.
neurips-1996-a-convergence-proof-for-the.tldr: The paper proves convergence for the most general form of the softassign quadratic assignment algorithm.

paragraphs: When the two eyes receive different scenes, perception can alternate between them. This phenomenon, binocular rivalry, raises a question about what is competing inside the visual system. The paper tests the hypothesis that one component of this alternation comes from competition between cortical interpretations of the sensory evidence.

Under this account, the competing entities are top-down explanations for what the eyes see. The proposal connects binocular rivalry with other situations in which the same sensory evidence supports two alternating percepts. Psychophysical evidence motivates investigating this shared explanatory mechanism, rather than treating rivalry solely as competition between the signals entering through the two eyes.

The authors extend their model into a hierarchy to address a further observation from neurophysiology. Some neurons receiving information from both eyes change their activity with the current percept, while others do not, even when they distinguish the presented stimuli. The hierarchy is intended to accommodate these different relationships between neural activity and perception. The contribution is therefore a model linking competing interpretations to both perceptual alternation and varied neural responses.
neurips-1996-a-hierarchical-model-of-vis.tldr: A hierarchical model explores whether binocular rivalry arises from competition between cortical interpretations of visual input.

paragraphs: The paper adapts a learning rule to neurons that communicate through spikes. Many learning rules describe inputs and outputs as continuously varying quantities. Biological action potentials instead have discrete amplitudes, with analog information carried by the intervals between events. This difference matters when translating learning mechanisms into hardware that uses spike representations.

The authors modify a rule based on the Riccati equation so that it works with action-potential outputs. They implement and demonstrate the resulting time-dependent rule in an analog VLSI chip. The chip stores synaptic weights using volatile capacitive storage, making the learning mechanism part of a physical electronic implementation.

The demonstrated rule achieves approximate weight normalization and detects temporal correlations in spike trains. The first result concerns keeping the collective scale of the weights controlled; the second concerns learning from relationships in event timing. Together, these findings show that a relatively simple rule can support useful learning behavior when outputs are spikes. The hardware demonstration connects the mathematical adaptation directly to a neuromorphic circuit.
neurips-1996-a-spike-based-learning-neur.tldr: A spike-compatible learning rule implemented in analog hardware approximately normalizes weights and detects temporal correlations.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to decide which combinations of traffic a packet data link can accept while still meeting quality-of-service requirements. The method learns a neural network decision function from observed service outcomes at different traffic loads. Its purpose is to turn those observations into a rule for admitting or rejecting proposed loads.

The central difficulty is a significant bias in earlier approaches of this kind. According to the abstract, that bias is likely in real systems and can lead to accepting traffic whose service outcomes miss targets by orders of magnitude. The authors preprocess the observations either to remove the bias or to provide a confidence level for the decision.

Applied to sources constructed from difficult-to-analyze Ethernet traces, the method produces an accurate access-control function and substantially outperforms analytic alternatives. A striking finding is that success depends on discarding more than 99% of the data. This makes data preparation central to the contribution: the usefulness of the learned decision rule depends on addressing bias in the observations, rather than simply retaining every available sample.
neurips-1996-adaptive-access-control-app.tldr: Bias-aware preprocessing enables a neural access-control rule to meet service targets on Ethernet-derived traffic.

paragraphs: A winner-take-all circuit selects the largest input by allowing one cell to remain active while suppressing the others. This paper modifies that familiar computation so that selection also depends on how inputs change over time. The aim is to make the input derivative, or rate of change, an important influence on which cell wins.

The authors add floating-gate transistors to a classic winner-take-all circuit. These components gradually cancel their inputs, introducing adaptation into a circuit otherwise concerned with comparing current input levels. As a result, the history of an input affects its influence on competition: a sustained signal is progressively treated differently from a changing one.

The circuit was designed, fabricated in a standard CMOS process, and tested, with a simplified analysis and experimental data presented. Saliency maps motivate the adaptation, connecting winner selection with the question of which signals attract attention. The contribution is a physical modification of competitive circuitry that adds temporal sensitivity while retaining the basic function of selecting among competing inputs.
neurips-1996-an-adaptive-wta-using-float.tldr: Floating-gate transistors add adaptation to a winner-take-all circuit, making input changes influence winner selection.

paragraphs: This paper implements a one-dimensional visual tracking chip using neuromorphic analog circuitry. The system models selective visual attention as part of controlling two kinds of eye movement: rapid shifts toward a target and smooth movements that follow it. Attention supplies the choice of which visual feature the system should track.

The chip processes the image at the focal plane to calculate saliency, a signal indicating which features should attract selection. A winner-take-all circuit then chooses a feature for tracking. As that target moves across the sensor array, the chip reports both its position and its direction of motion, linking feature selection to information needed for movement control.

The authors demonstrate the chip in a closed-loop system with a one-dimensional mechanical eye. The system performs both saccadic and smooth pursuit tracking movements. This demonstration matters because the selected visual information is used to drive an actual moving device, completing the connection between sensing, attention, and action. The reported implementation and demonstration operate along one dimension.
neurips-1996-analog-vlsi-circuits-for-at.tldr: An analog visual chip selects salient features and guides a one-dimensional mechanical eye through rapid and smooth tracking movements.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes temporal-difference learning when it estimates a Markov chain's cost-to-go function using a linear function approximator. The cost-to-go describes the future cost associated with a state. Instead of representing every state's value independently, the method adjusts a parameter vector that determines the approximation.

The analysis follows online parameter updates along a single endless trajectory. Its stated setting is a finite-state Markov chain that is irreducible and aperiodic: all states communicate, and transitions are not locked into a fixed repeating period. Within this setting, the authors establish convergence with probability one, characterize the limiting approximation, and bound its approximation error.

These results address three connected questions: whether learning settles, what it settles on, and how far that result can be from the desired function. The paper also introduces a line of reasoning intended to clarify the learning dynamics. Two counterexamples inform discussion of why online updating and linear parameterization matter, keeping these architectural and procedural choices central to the interpretation of the guarantees.
neurips-1996-analysis-of-temporal-difffe.tldr: The paper establishes convergence, a limiting solution, and an error bound for online temporal-difference learning with linear approximation.

paragraphs: Analog neural circuits can lose accuracy because manufacturing leaves individual electronic devices with differing characteristics. This paper addresses that practical obstacle through dynamic control. Its goal is to let a silicon neural network compensate for device variation while also adapting when the steady input level changes.

The authors apply their architecture to a fabricated CMOS winner-take-all chip. Such a circuit compares competing inputs and selects a winner, so unintended input offsets can distort the comparison. Compensating for these offset voltages addresses a concrete way in which the physical circuit can depart from its intended computation.

Experimental data show that the proposed control architecture is effective in this implementation. The significance lies in making adaptation part of the hardware's operation, allowing the circuit to respond to device characteristics and input conditions. The paper therefore connects a broad obstacle for analog neural systems with a demonstrated corrective mechanism on a specific chip. Its reported evidence concerns compensation in that fabricated winner-take-all implementation.
neurips-1996-dynamically-adaptable-cmos-.tldr: Dynamic control compensates for device offsets and changing input levels in a fabricated analog winner-take-all chip.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how combining classifiers can improve phoneme classification, a component of speech recognition. The central issue is how the individual classifiers are organized and combined. An ensemble can contain several predictors, but the rule connecting their predictions is itself an important part of the method.

The authors examine boosting and mixtures of experts, studying each approach separately and also in combination. They compare these principled ensemble strategies with simpler approaches such as averaging. This setup asks whether a more structured way of building and combining predictors offers benefits beyond the presence of multiple classifiers alone.

Results are reported on two speech databases: one involving isolated words and another involving continuous speech with a large vocabulary. Across the reported comparisons, boosting and mixtures provide better performance than the more naive ensemble methods. The finding supports paying attention to ensemble design when improving phoneme classifiers. It also places the evidence in two distinct speech settings, while keeping the evaluated task focused on phoneme classification.
neurips-1996-ensemble-methods-for-phonem.tldr: Boosting and mixtures of experts improve phoneme classification more effectively than simple ensemble averaging.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to compare regression models through their equivalent kernels. These kernels provide a description of how a fitted model uses data when making predictions. The intended framework spans neural networks as well as parametric and nonparametric statistical methods, giving different model families a common basis for examination.

Existing techniques encounter problems when a model contains multiple layers of adjustable parameters, as neural networks do. The authors propose estimating equivalent kernels by perturbing the data and examining the model's response. This approach is designed to overcome the difficulty posed by layered parameterizations and make the comparison framework usable for neural networks.

Experiments indicate that the networks use fewer than the maximum available degrees of freedom, and that regularization can control this effective flexibility. The estimated kernels also differ in size and shape across regions of the input space. These findings describe networks as adapting their regression behavior locally, rather than applying one uniform pattern everywhere. The method therefore helps expose both effective model complexity and variation in how predictions are formed.
neurips-1996-estimating-equivalent-kerne.tldr: Data perturbations reveal neural networks' equivalent kernels, exposing controllable effective complexity and locally varying regression behavior.

paragraphs: This paper combines two techniques that improve different aspects of a support vector machine. The virtual support vector method improves generalization by incorporating known invariances: changes to an input that should leave the correct prediction unchanged. The reduced set method speeds up prediction by approximating the machine's decision surface.

On 10,000 NIST test digit images, incorporating invariances lowers the error rate from 1.4% to 1.0%. Applying the reduced set method then makes prediction fifty times faster than with the virtual support vector machine. These results distinguish the accuracy benefit of incorporating problem knowledge from the speed benefit of simplifying the resulting decision computation.

The combined machine achieves 1.1% error and runs 22 times faster than the original machine. Thus, the final approximation retains an accuracy improvement while also reducing prediction cost. The two techniques have different stated scopes: virtual support vectors require known invariances in the problem, whereas the reduced set method applies to any support vector machine. Their combination shows how those complementary improvements can operate together.
neurips-1996-improving-the-accuracy-and-.tldr: Combining known invariances with decision-surface approximation produces an SVM that is 22 times faster and more accurate than the original.

paragraphs: This paper examines self-organizing maps as tools for two related tasks: representing data through clusters or representative vectors, and arranging data to display its structure. It reviews empirical findings and relevant theory about their limitations. The broader question is whether one map performs both jobs well enough to justify combining them in a single method.

The authors introduce an alternative that pairs online K-means clustering with Sammon mapping of the cluster centers. This separates the construction of representative groups from the arrangement of those representatives. The combined technique directly challenges the argument that self-organizing maps retain a special advantage because they perform vector quantization and multidimensional scaling together.

A comprehensive empirical study uses a series of clustering problems based on multivariate normal distributions. In those comparisons, self-organizing maps perform significantly worse in quantization error, recovery of cluster structure, and preservation of topology. The results concern both accurate representation and faithful organization of the data. They support the proposed combination as a stronger approach on the studied problems.
neurips-1996-limitations-of-self-organiz.tldr: Online K-means followed by Sammon mapping outperforms self-organizing maps on the studied clustering and structure-preservation tasks.

paragraphs: The paper addresses blind source separation: recovering independent source signals from observations that mix them together. Its setting has equal numbers of sources and observed signals, with an unknown square matrix of causal linear filters describing the mixing. The desired result is a linear operation that untangles these filtered combinations.

The authors formulate separation as maximum-likelihood density estimation and introduce Contextual ICA. The algorithm searches for independent components using both temporal information and relationships across the observed signals. They also show that the Infomax algorithm is a special case, placing the new method within a broader formulation of independent component analysis.

Using temporal structure allows Contextual ICA to separate signals in several situations where standard methods cannot. The stated cases include sources with low kurtosis, colored Gaussian sources, and sources whose histograms are Gaussian. The key distinction is that a histogram describes signal values without fully describing their organization through time. By using that additional organization, the method gains separation information beyond what the distribution of individual values provides.
neurips-1996-maximum-likelihood-blind-so.tldr: Contextual ICA uses temporal and spatial information to separate sources that standard ICA methods cannot handle.

paragraphs: This paper studies how prior knowledge about a function's direction of change can help a learning system. A monotonicity hint says that increasing certain inputs should move the output consistently in one direction. Such knowledge supplements the training examples by describing a relationship the learned function is expected to respect.

The authors define a measure of monotonicity error for a candidate function. This makes violations of the hint something that can be assessed during learning. They then derive an objective for enforcing monotonicity from Bayesian principles, connecting the side information to a formal learning criterion rather than leaving it as an informal preference.

The approach is demonstrated on a credit card application task and a medical diagnosis problem. Using the hints produces statistically significant performance improvements on both. These findings show that directional knowledge can be useful training information in practical prediction tasks. The applicable premise is that the target function is monotonic in some or all of the relevant inputs; the hint expresses that substantive knowledge about the problem.
neurips-1996-monotonicity-hints-88aa054f.tldr: A Bayesian objective incorporates monotonicity knowledge and significantly improves performance on two real-world prediction tasks.

paragraphs: This paper introduces learning rules for independent component analysis and blind source separation. The organizing idea is to give each individual neuron the job of finding one independent component. A neuron learns to act as a separator, turning mixed observations into an output corresponding to one of their underlying independent sources.

The proposed rules use simple constrained Hebbian or anti-Hebbian learning, with the option of adding decorrelating feedback. These mechanisms define how the separator adapts while imposing structure on the learning process. The one-unit formulation focuses the learning task on extracting a single component, making that unit the central building block of the approach.

The authors also introduce a computationally efficient fixed-point algorithm to accelerate convergence of the stochastic gradient rules. This adds a second contribution alongside the learning formulation: a faster way to reach the separator sought by the updates. The abstract presents the fixed-point method as a response to convergence speed, linking the design of the learning rule with the practicality of carrying out the resulting computation.
neurips-1996-one-unit-learning-rules-for.tldr: One-unit ICA rules learn individual source separators, with a fixed-point algorithm introduced to accelerate convergence.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes online learning when examples come from a finite training set and the learning rate is not infinitesimally small. It studies a linear network with many weights, extending statistical mechanics methods to obtain exact results for how generalization error changes during training. This connects the learning trajectory to performance on unseen examples.

One finding concerns small training sets whose size is comparable to the number of weights. In this setting, larger learning rates can be used without sacrificing either eventual generalization performance or convergence speed. The result ties the consequences of the learning rate to the finite supply of training examples.

The authors also consider choosing settings for a specified final training time. With an optimal learning rate, and with weight decay playing a less important role, online learning generalizes essentially as well as offline learning. This is a result within the analyzed linear-network setting. It shows that carefully chosen online updates can match offline generalization even when the available training time is part of the optimization problem.
neurips-1996-online-learning-from-finite.tldr: An exact linear-network analysis shows that well-tuned online learning from finite datasets can generalize essentially as well as offline learning.

paragraphs: The paper develops a theoretical framework for interpreting population codes, in which information is represented across a collection of neurons. Its key extension is to let the population communicate a probability distribution over an underlying quantity. This expands the interpretation beyond representing just one particular value of that quantity.

A probability distribution can describe how support is spread across possible values. Interpreting a population in this way therefore changes what one asks of the code: the issue becomes how neural activity represents a range of possibilities and their relative probabilities. The framework is designed to make this richer form of representation part of a unified theoretical treatment.

The authors use the framework to analyze two existing models and to propose and evaluate a third model for encoding distributions. This gives the theory a concrete comparative role, as well as a role in constructing a new encoding approach. The contribution is a way to reason about population activity as probabilistic information, supported by analysis of multiple candidate models.
neurips-1996-probabilistic-interpretatio.tldr: A theoretical framework interprets neural population activity as encoding probability distributions and uses that view to examine three models.

paragraphs: Stochastic learning can progress faster than batch learning, but randomness in individual weight updates becomes an obstacle late in training. A conventional response is to gradually reduce the learning rate. The paper asks whether increasing the batch size provides another way to suppress this noise and improve convergence.

The analysis examines least mean squares learning with two alternatives: batches that remain small and fixed, and batches whose size adapts during training. Increasing a batch means using more input presentations to form an update. The relevant comparison therefore measures convergence against the total number of input presentations, rather than only the number of updates.

The authors find that the best adaptive schedule increases batch size exponentially. Even with this schedule, the best mean-square convergence rate is proportional to 1/T, where T counts input presentations. This matches the rate available through learning-rate annealing. The result gives adaptive batching a precise role as an alternative means of removing update noise, while showing that it does not improve this asymptotic rate in the analyzed setting.
neurips-1996-removing-noise-in-on-line-s.tldr: For least mean squares learning, exponentially increasing batch sizes match the best 1/T convergence rate of learning-rate annealing.

paragraphs: This paper examines what time-delay neural networks can represent and how effectively they learn sequence problems. It compares two architectures: networks with delays only on their inputs and networks that also place delays on hidden units. The distinction concerns where information from earlier times remains available during processing.

Both architectures can represent the same class of languages, identified as definite memory machine languages. Thus, moving delays into the hidden part of the network does not expand the language class in the stated comparison. This result separates representational capacity from the practical question of how readily an architecture learns particular patterns.

The networks with hidden-unit delays perform better on problems built from features that repeat within short time windows. This shows that architecture can affect learning performance even when the compared networks have the same stated representational reach. The advantage is tied to the temporal structure of the tasks: repeated local features favor retaining information at the hidden-unit level. The contribution combines a capacity comparison with a finding about which delay arrangement better suits those problems.
neurips-1996-representation-and-inductio.tldr: Hidden-unit delays improve learning of repeated short-window features even though both compared architectures represent the same language class.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many hidden units a neural network needs to fit a finite collection of real-valued samples exactly. The architecture is a feedforward network with one hidden layer and several outputs. Exact learning here concerns matching the supplied samples, making network size the central object of analysis.

The authors hold the training set fixed and treat the network as a function of its weights. This shifts attention to whether suitable parameter choices can produce all the required outputs. For a broad family of transfer functions, they derive both a lower bound and an upper bound on the necessary number of hidden units.

The bounds depend on the number of samples and the dimensions of the input and output spaces. Together, they constrain the range of network sizes relevant to exact fitting: the lower bound expresses a size requirement, while the upper bound provides a sufficient size guarantee. The contribution is an analytic characterization of representational requirements for the stated architecture, connecting dataset dimensions to hidden-layer capacity.
neurips-1996-size-of-multilayer-networks.tldr: The paper derives lower and upper bounds on hidden-layer size for exactly fitting finite real-valued datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies relationships across both space and time in naturally changing images. Its motivating hypothesis is that visual processing seeks an efficient representation by decorrelating the incoming signal. Decorrelation means reducing predictable statistical relationships between parts of the signal, so the representation carries less repeated information.

The authors measure the spatiotemporal power spectrum of natural image sequences. This describes how the signal's power is distributed across patterns of spatial variation and temporal change. From that measured structure, they analytically derive the transformation needed to decorrelate the input. The proposed processing operation is therefore grounded in the statistics of the visual material.

They then compare the derived transformation with visual processing observed in psychophysical experiments. This creates a connection between properties of natural images and measured human visual sensitivities. The paper's contribution is the sequence of measurement, analytic prediction, and comparison: an efficient-coding hypothesis becomes a specific transformation that can be assessed against perception. The abstract presents this as an investigation of the hypothesis without specifying the degree of agreement.
neurips-1996-spatiotemporal-coupling-and.tldr: The paper derives a decorrelating transform from natural image statistics and compares it with human visual processing.

paragraphs: This paper introduces support vector regression, applying the support-vector concept to predicting numerical outputs. Its focus is regression rather than assigning inputs to discrete categories. The authors investigate the technique through comparisons with other regression approaches, placing the new formulation alongside established ways of learning real-valued relationships.

The comparisons include bagging based on regression trees and ridge regression performed in feature space. Bagging is considered as a committee regression technique, providing a comparison with a method that combines multiple predictors. The feature-space ridge regression comparison supplies another point of reference for evaluating the support-vector approach.

Based on the experiments, the authors expect support vector regression to offer advantages in high-dimensional spaces. Their stated reason is that its optimization does not depend on the dimensionality of the input space. The conclusion is framed as an expectation motivated by the experiments and this optimization property. The main contribution combines the introduction of the regression technique with an argument for why it could be especially useful when inputs have many dimensions.
neurips-1996-support-vector-regression-m.tldr: The paper introduces support vector regression and argues that its optimization structure makes it promising for high-dimensional inputs.

paragraphs: This paper examines natural sounds to understand the statistical structure that an efficient auditory system might exploit. The authors analyze several sound ensembles using a filter bank, separating sounds into frequency bands. They focus on amplitude and phase within those bands and describe their distributions and power spectra.

Simple parametric descriptions apply across very different sound types. In particular, the amplitude distribution has an exponential tail, while its power spectrum follows a modified power law. The latter behavior appears as self-similarity and long-range temporal correlations: relationships in the sound persist across extended time separations and exhibit structure across scales.

Within a given sound ensemble, the statistics are also nearly identical across frequency bands. The authors interpret this as suggesting translation invariance along the cochlear axis. Together, the findings indicate substantial redundancy in natural sounds, including repeated statistical structure across time and frequency. This supports investigating auditory neural codes in relation to the regularities of their inputs, while the implications for the actual neural code remain proposals motivated by the measurements.
neurips-1996-temporal-low-order-statisti.tldr: Natural sounds share temporal and frequency-band regularities that reveal redundancy potentially relevant to auditory coding.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to judge the predictive cost of choosing a model that learns quickly. With unlimited computation, the proposed ideal is to select a model and its parameters by minimizing expected generalization error. In practical choices, however, faster learning may justify giving up some performance on unseen data.

The authors set out a method for quantifying this departure from the ideal. That turns a loose preference for speed into a more explicit tradeoff: a model can be evaluated in terms of the generalization performance sacrificed to obtain faster learning. The method is intended to support an informed choice between those competing priorities.

Its scope includes a broad class of models, particularly very fast memory-based methods such as RAMnets. The abstract identifies an additional contribution for these methods: a way to analyze their generalization properties within a Bayesian framework. This connects fast memory-based learning to a formal account of expected predictive performance. The paper's significance lies in making the cost of computational convenience something that can be analyzed rather than merely assumed.
neurips-1996-the-generalisation-cost-of-.tldr: A Bayesian analysis quantifies the generalization performance sacrificed for faster learning in RAMnets and other models.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a stochastic gradient descent algorithm aimed at improving convergence late in optimization. Its main mechanism is a nonlinear adaptive momentum scheme. Momentum carries information from previous updates into subsequent ones, and here that mechanism adapts to make effective use of the objective's curvature.

Curvature describes how the slope of the objective changes as the parameters move. Using this information can help determine how updates should behave as optimization progresses. The proposed algorithm incorporates it while requiring only O(n) storage and computation, so both costs grow linearly with the number of parameters rather than requiring a full pairwise description of curvature.

The authors report convergence rates close to the theoretical optimum and demonstrate the technique on linear networks and large nonlinear networks trained by backpropagation. The contribution combines a targeted improvement in late-stage convergence with a modest computational requirement. This matters because the benefit of a more informed update rule must be considered alongside its cost: the reported method seeks faster progress without making each update prohibitively expensive.
neurips-1996-using-curvature-information.tldr: Adaptive momentum uses curvature information to approach optimal late-stage stochastic convergence with linear storage and computation.
